title: Classic Vitamin Deficiencies: B12 vs Folate, Pellagra, Scurvy, Beriberi and Rickets
summary: Learn why methylmalonic acid separates vitamin B12 from folate deficiency, why folate alone is dangerous when nerves are involved, and how to recognise pellagra, scurvy, thiamine deficiency and rickets or osteomalacia, with their lab clues.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 27 Hits 1 (B12 neurologic damage, folate does not relieve it, MMA and homocysteine), 4 (pellagra) and 5 (scurvy, beriberi, rickets vs osteomalacia) and Exam Trap 1 (megaloblastic anemia treated with folate). Checked against Hannibal 2016, Wolffenbuttel 2019, Savvidou 2014, Feuz 2023, Gandhi 2023, Marrs 2021 and Uday 2017 (all full text via Europe PMC). Nuances: the sources describe B12 neurologic damage as often permanent and at least partly irreversible rather than always irreversible (rv-b12-neuro-irreversible-overstated); MMA also rises in renal impairment (rv-mma-renal-confounder); the Wernicke triad is confusion, ocular signs and ataxia, with confabulation belonging to Korsakoff syndrome and the full triad seen in a minority (rv-wernicke-triad-confabulation); osteomalacia is not only an adult disease, since it accompanies rickets in growing children (rv-osteomalacia-not-adults-only). Not taught (pending): the folate and B12 Number Vault cutoffs, B12 stores of 3–6 years, and a mechanism for folate worsening neuropathy.

objectives: Explain why methylmalonic acid rises in vitamin B12 deficiency but not in folate deficiency, while homocysteine rises in both.
State why folate alone is unsafe when megaloblastic anemia comes with neurologic signs, and that nerve damage can occur without anemia.
Recognise pellagra, scurvy, thiamine deficiency and rickets or osteomalacia from their classic features and lab clues.

scenes.title: Four patients, four vitamins
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four patient cards. (1) A 70-year-old woman with macrocytic anemia and numb feet, already started on folic acid. (2) A man with heavy alcohol use, a scaly rash on sun-exposed skin and diarrhea. (3) A man on a poor diet with bleeding gums, painful swollen knees and a wound that will not heal. (4) A toddler with bowed legs. Question token: “Which vitamin, and which lab clue?”

cues.text: Four invented patients. A seventy-year-old woman with macrocytic anemia and numb feet, already started on folic acid.
A man who drinks heavily, with a rash on sun-exposed skin and diarrhea. A man with bleeding gums, painful swollen knees and a wound that will not heal. And a toddler with bowed legs.
Which vitamin is missing in each, and which lab clue would you look for?

props.label: Which vitamin, and which lab clue?

scenes.title: Two enzymes, two markers
scenes.altText: Schematic: two enzyme cards. Methionine synthase converts homocysteine to methionine and needs vitamin B12; folate deficiency also raises homocysteine. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA and needs B12 but not other one-carbon vitamins. Result cards: low B12 → homocysteine and methylmalonic acid (MMA) both rise; low folate → homocysteine rises, MMA normal. Both deficiencies can cause megaloblastic anemia.

cues.text: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for two enzymes. Methionine synthase turns homocysteine into methionine, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase turns methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA.
When B12 runs short, both substrates back up: homocysteine rises, and so does methylmalonic acid, MMA.
Folate deficiency also raises homocysteine, but the mutase step does not depend on folate, so MMA stays normal. That makes MMA the more specific marker of B12 deficiency.
Both B12 and folate deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia, so the anemia alone cannot tell them apart.

scenes.title: When folate hides B12
scenes.altText: Card “Nerves, not just blood”: B12 deficiency can damage the nervous system — subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal columns), often leaving permanent disability; neurologic or psychiatric disease can occur with no anemia or macrocytosis (a classic series of 40 patients). Card “Folate alone”: folate therapy may mask the anemia while untreated B12 deficiency lets nerve damage continue or accelerate. Caveat token: MMA also rises in renal failure; normal B12 and MMA do not exclude symptomatic deficiency.

cues.text: B12 deficiency is not only a blood disease. It can damage the nervous system, including subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord’s dorsal columns, which often leaves permanent disability.
Nerve or psychiatric disease can even appear without anemia or macrocytosis. One classic series described forty such patients.
That is patient one’s danger. Folate therapy may mask the anemia, while the untreated B12 deficiency lets the nerve damage continue, or even accelerate. She needs B12 testing and B12 treatment.
Two caveats. MMA also rises when kidney function is poor, and normal B12 and MMA results do not fully exclude a symptomatic deficiency.

props.label: MMA ↑ in kidney failure · normal B12/MMA ≠ excluded

scenes.title: Four more deficiency pictures
scenes.altText: Four cards. Pellagra (niacin, B3): photosensitive dermatitis (Casal’s necklace), diarrhea, dementia, death; risks include alcoholism, corn-based diets, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, isoniazid. Scurvy (vitamin C): collagen hydroxylation fails — bleeding gums, arthralgia or hemarthrosis, poor wound healing; coagulation tests usually normal; serum vitamin C < 11.4 µmol/L = substantial deficiency. Thiamine (B1): wet beriberi = high-output heart failure with edema; dry beriberi = neuropathy; Wernicke = confusion, eye signs, ataxia (full triad uncommon); Korsakoff adds confabulation, memory loss; whole-blood thiamine diphosphate. Rickets/osteomalacia: rickets = defective growth-plate mineralization; osteomalacia = defective mineralization of existing bone (adults and children with rickets); PTH ↑, ALP ↑, phosphate ↓, calcium normal until late; 25(OH)D for vitamin D status.

cues.text: Patient two has pellagra, from niacin deficiency: photosensitive dermatitis such as Casal’s necklace, diarrhea, dementia, and death if untreated. Risks include alcoholism, corn-based diets, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome and isoniazid.

Patient three has scurvy. Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate collagen, so gums bleed, joints ache or bleed, and wounds heal poorly, yet clotting tests are usually normal. Serum vitamin C below 11.4 micromoles per litre marks substantial deficiency.

Thiamine deficiency: wet beriberi is high-output heart failure with edema, dry beriberi is neuropathy, and Wernicke encephalopathy is confusion, eye signs and ataxia, though few patients show all three. Korsakoff syndrome adds confabulation and memory loss.

Patient four has rickets: defective mineralization at open growth plates. Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of existing bone, in adults and in children with rickets. PTH and alkaline phosphatase rise, phosphate falls, and calcium stays normal until late.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Megaloblastic anemia — just give folate” (✓ check B12 and MMA first; folate may mask B12 deficiency while nerve damage continues); “No anemia, so not B12 deficiency” (✓ nerve damage can occur without anemia or macrocytosis); “Osteomalacia is only an adult disease” (✓ children with rickets have osteomalacia too).

cues.text: Trap one: megaloblastic anemia, so just give folate. No: check B12 and MMA first, because folate may mask a B12 deficiency while the nerves keep failing.
Trap two: no anemia, so it cannot be B12 deficiency. No: nerve damage can appear without anemia or macrocytosis.
Trap three: osteomalacia is only an adult disease. No: children with rickets have osteomalacia of their existing bone too.

props.title: ✗ “Osteomalacia = adults only.”
lines: ✓ Children with rickets have it too

scenes.title: Two drains, one plumber
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “B12 is the plumber for two drains — the homocysteine drain and the MMA drain. Folate helps clear only the homocysteine drain. If the MMA drain backs up, call B12.” Tokens: Hcy drain = B12 + folate · MMA drain = B12 only · MMA backed up → think B12. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: B12 is the plumber for two drains, homocysteine and MMA. Folate helps clear only the homocysteine drain. If the MMA drain backs up, call B12.

Where it breaks: poor kidney function also backs up MMA; a normal MMA does not fully exclude B12 deficiency; and homocysteine also rises with vitamin B6 deficiency, kidney disease, hypothyroidism and some drugs.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “MMA ↑ + homocysteine ↑ → B12 · homocysteine ↑ alone → folate · nerves need B12”, “4 D’s → niacin · gums and joints → vitamin C · heart or Wernicke → thiamine · rickets + osteomalacia → mineralization”.

cues.text: A raised methylmalonic acid with raised homocysteine points to vitamin B12 rather than folate deficiency, so neurologic signs need B12 and not folate alone, while the 4 Ds point to niacin, bleeding gums to vitamin C, beriberi or Wernicke signs to thiamine, and rickets with osteomalacia to failed bone mineralization.

props.label: MMA ↑ + Hcy ↑ → B12 · Hcy ↑ alone → folate · nerves need B12
4 Ds → niacin · gums → vitamin C · beriberi → thiamine · bones → mineralization

explanation.what: Plain language: B12 and folate both help make DNA, so lacking either gives the same large, immature red cells, but only B12 also protects the nerves and only B12 is needed to clear methylmalonic acid. Niacin, vitamin C and thiamine deficiencies and poor bone mineralization each have their own classic picture. Scientific terms: methionine synthase, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, methylmalonic acid (MMA), total homocysteine, megaloblastic anemia, subacute combined degeneration, pellagra, Casal’s necklace, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, wet and dry beriberi, Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome, thiamine diphosphate, rickets, osteomalacia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
explanation.why: B12 is the cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency backs up homocysteine and MMA. Folate deficiency raises homocysteine only, because the mutase step does not use folate. Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate collagen, so vessels, gums and wounds fail. Calcium or vitamin D deprivation drives secondary hyperparathyroidism, renal phosphate loss and poor mineralization.
explanation.measure: B12: low serum B12 with raised MMA (and homocysteine); MMA also rises in renal impairment and normal values do not fully exclude deficiency. Folate: raised homocysteine, normal MMA. Scurvy: serum vitamin C < 11.4 µmol/L marks substantial deficiency; coagulation tests usually normal. Thiamine: whole-blood thiamine diphosphate, often by LC-MS/MS. Rickets/osteomalacia: PTH and alkaline phosphatase raised, phosphate low, calcium normal until compensation fails; 25(OH)D for vitamin D status.
explanation.differs: B12 (homocysteine and MMA raised, neurologic risk) vs folate (homocysteine raised, MMA normal); wet beriberi (high-output heart failure) vs dry beriberi (neuropathy) vs Wernicke (confusion, eye signs, ataxia) vs Korsakoff (confabulation, memory loss); rickets (growth plate) vs osteomalacia (existing bone, any age).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the next test before treating megaloblastic anemia with neurologic signs, the marker that separates B12 from folate deficiency, the 4 Ds of pellagra and its risk groups, scurvy with normal clotting tests, the Wernicke triad, and the biochemistry of nutritional rickets.

comparisons.title: B12 vs folate deficiency
comparisons.distinguisher: MMA rises in B12 deficiency (or renal impairment), not in folate deficiency.

comparisons.title: Rickets vs osteomalacia
comparisons.distinguisher: Where mineralization fails: growth plate vs remodelling bone.

mnemonic.text: Two drains, one plumber: B12 clears both the homocysteine drain and the MMA drain; folate helps only the homocysteine drain. If the MMA drain backs up, call B12.
mnemonic.explanation: Links the two B12-dependent enzymes to the two markers and shows why MMA is the more specific B12 marker.
mnemonic.limitation: Poor kidney function also raises MMA; a normal MMA does not fully exclude B12 deficiency; homocysteine also rises with vitamin B6 deficiency, kidney disease, hypothyroidism and some drugs.

analogyLimitations: Enzyme and patient cards are schematic.
The plumbing analogy ignores renal and other causes of raised MMA and homocysteine.
takeaway: A raised methylmalonic acid with raised homocysteine points to vitamin B12 rather than folate deficiency, so neurologic signs need B12 and not folate alone, while the 4 Ds point to niacin, bleeding gums to vitamin C, beriberi or Wernicke signs to thiamine, and rickets with osteomalacia to failed bone mineralization.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has macrocytic anemia, numb feet and an unsteady gait. Serum methylmalonic acid and total homocysteine are both raised, and kidney function is normal. Which is the best interpretation and plan?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency; treat with B12, not folate alone
options.rationale: Correct. Raised MMA with raised homocysteine and normal kidney function points to B12; folate alone may mask the anemia while nerve damage continues.

options.text: Folate deficiency; treat with folic acid alone
options.rationale: Incorrect. Folate deficiency raises homocysteine but not MMA, and folate alone is unsafe with neurologic signs.

options.text: Kidney failure explains the raised MMA; no vitamin problem
options.rationale: Incorrect. Kidney function is normal here, so the raised MMA with homocysteine and the neurologic signs point to B12 deficiency.

options.text: No deficiency, because neurologic signs need a very low hemoglobin
options.rationale: Incorrect. B12-related nerve damage can occur even without anemia or macrocytosis.

questions.stem: A toddler with bowed legs has nutritional rickets. Which biochemical pattern is most typical before compensation fails?

options.text: Raised PTH and alkaline phosphatase, low phosphate, normal calcium
options.rationale: Correct. Secondary hyperparathyroidism keeps calcium normal while causing renal phosphate loss; poor mineralization raises alkaline phosphatase.

options.text: Low PTH, high phosphate, low alkaline phosphatase
options.rationale: Incorrect. Calcium deprivation raises PTH, which lowers phosphate.
Incorrect. In nutritional rickets PTH rises and holds calcium normal, not high.

options.text: Normal PTH with low calcium from the start
options.rationale: Incorrect. PTH rises early and holds calcium normal until compensation fails.

questions.stem: A man with alcohol use disorder and a poor diet has bleeding swollen gums, perifollicular hemorrhages and slow wound healing. PT and aPTT are normal. Which deficiency is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate collagen; scurvy causes gum bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhage and poor healing, usually with normal coagulation tests.
Incorrect. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, not the gum, skin and wound changes of failed collagen synthesis.
Incorrect. Niacin deficiency (pellagra) gives photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia.
Incorrect. Thiamine deficiency gives beriberi (heart failure or neuropathy) and Wernicke encephalopathy, not collagen-type bleeding.

claims.text: B12-dependent enzymes; homocysteine raised in B12 and folate deficiency; MMA raised in B12 but not folate deficiency; both cause megaloblastic anemia.
B12 neurologic damage (subacute combined degeneration) often permanent; can occur without anemia or macrocytosis.
Folate therapy may mask the anemia while untreated B12 deficiency lets nerve damage continue or accelerate.
claims.note: The review states this as well known and cites older literature; no mechanism is taught.

claims.text: MMA raised in renal impairment; normal B12 and MMA do not fully exclude deficiency; other causes of raised homocysteine.
Pellagra: niacin deficiency, 4 Ds, Casal’s necklace, risk groups (alcoholism, corn diets, Hartnup, carcinoid, isoniazid).
Scurvy: collagen hydroxylation, gums, joints, wounds, perifollicular hemorrhage; normal coagulation tests; serum vitamin C < 11.4 µmol/L.
Wet beriberi high-output heart failure; dry beriberi neuropathy; Wernicke triad, full triad uncommon; Korsakoff confabulation.
Rickets vs osteomalacia definitions; osteomalacia in children with rickets; PTH and ALP up, phosphate down, calcium normal until late; 25(OH)D for status.
Reviewer details not taught: Number Vault cutoffs for B12 and folate, B12 stores of 3–6 years, and a mechanism by which folate worsens neuropathy.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson; not verified against an external source here.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 27 Hit 1 and Exam Trap 1 call B12 neurologic damage irreversible. Wolffenbuttel 2019 says subacute combined degeneration often leads to permanent disability and describes patients improving with treatment; Hannibal 2016 says at least some consequences are irreversible. The lesson teaches “often permanent” (register flag rv-b12-neuro-irreversible-overstated).

Ch. 27 Hit 1 and Exam Trap 1 present methylmalonate as specific for B12 deficiency without the renal caveat. Hannibal 2016 and Wolffenbuttel 2019 note MMA rises in renal impairment, and normal MMA does not fully exclude deficiency (register flag rv-mma-renal-confounder).

Ch. 27 Hit 5 lists Wernicke-Korsakoff as ataxia, ophthalmoplegia and confabulation. Marrs 2021 gives the Wernicke triad as confusion, ocular abnormalities and ataxia, places confabulation in Korsakoff syndrome, and notes only 16% of an autopsy series had the full triad (register flag rv-wernicke-triad-confabulation).

Ch. 27 Hit 5 says rickets = kids and osteomalacia = adults. Uday 2017 states osteomalacia always accompanies rickets in growing children and is not just an adult disease; nutritional rickets can also come from low calcium intake (register flag rv-osteomalacia-not-adults-only).
